sections.html:
• Common names: Leopard shrimp, Leopard Tiger shrimp, Armadillo shrimp, Red-spotted shrimp
  • Minimum tank size: 40 litres
  • Breeding: difficult
  • Optimal KH: 0–4
  • Optimal TDS: 80–150 µS/cm or 40–80 ppm
  • Nitrate: less than 10 ppm
  • Diet: algae eater/omnivore
  • Temperament: peaceful
  • Colour: semi-transparent body with small reddish to black dots

Leopard shrimp are not for beginners. Caridina rubropunctata is more difficult to keep than most other shrimp species. They have very specific needs: clean water, good water flow and a low temperature. They are very sensitive and need very stable water parameters and plenty of oxygen. Knowledge of these dwarf shrimp is scanty. They are rare and have only very rarely made their way into the trade.

They can be confused with young Amano shrimp, which are bigger and rounder.

If you are buying captive-bred (for several generations) shrimp, find out the water parameters they were bred in. If you can't find this information, presume that the breeder kept them in parameters close to the natural ones and replicate them.

Caridina rubropunctata has a very limited distribution range. It is found only in the north of Vietnam (Thai Nguyen, Dong Hy, Van Lang). The species was discovered in 2007 and described only in 2011. The name rubropunctata combines the Latin words for 'red' and 'spotted', so it means red-spotted.
These shrimp are typically found in rivers and spring-fed streams in a mountainous region, where the water is generally soft and cool.

Although these shrimp do not require a lot of space, the minimum recommended tank size is 40 litres. Small tanks make it difficult to control water parameters constantly, and things can go wrong very quickly. A larger tank is always preferable for the stability of water chemistry.

Do not add Leopard shrimp to a tank that is not cycled yet: high ammonia and nitrates will kill them. The most important factor is a stable nitrogen cycle.

They are not hardy and are very sensitive to even small changes in water values, so acclimate them slowly; 2–3 hours is generally enough.

Decorations are not necessary, but leaves, rocks, driftwood, PVC pipes and similar items provide hiding places and surface area for algae and biofilm.

• Temperature: 20–22 °C. These shrimp are sensitive to temperature fluctuations.
  • pH: slightly acidic, 6.0–6.8.
  • Hardness: they do not like hard water; 4–8 GH and 0–4 KH.
  • TDS: 80–150 µS/cm or 40–80 ppm.

They require excellent water quality, so tap water is not suitable; only RO/DI water is recommended. RO water has no minerals, so pH, KH, GH and TDS must be set manually with shrimp re-mineralizers.

They need a well-oxygenated tank with good water flow, since the species lives in streams and rivers. An extra air pump may be needed; low oxygen can be a real problem.

Lighting: no special requirements, as they are nocturnal and do not really depend on light. If you have plants, adapt lighting to their needs.

Substrate: an active substrate is needed to keep pH below 7.0, for example ADA Amazonia aqua soil, Fluval Plant and Shrimp Stratum or Akadama-Bonsai soil.

Filtration: sponge or matten filters are recommended. They are cheap, easy to maintain, provide plenty of grazing surface and are safe for baby shrimp.

Leopard shrimp are omnivores. They feed on dead animal and plant matter as well as commercial foods, and are good scavengers that clean up algae, biofilm, debris and waste.

For best growth they need a mix of meat and vegetation, with protein at about 20–30% of the diet.

Suggested foods:

  • leaves
  • plants
  • blanched vegetables
  • crushed snails
  • frozen bloodworms
  • brine shrimp
  • Dennerle Shrimp King
  • Hikari Shrimp Cuisine
  • Glassgarden Shrimp Dinner Food Pads

Dry leaves and blanched vegetables (carrot, sprouts, spinach, cucumber, zucchini) supply the microelements needed for molting.

Calcium is essential for the exoskeleton, and molting leaves shrimp vulnerable, so provide enough calcium through specialized invertebrate foods or calcium-rich vegetables.

In a matured tank (with algae and biofilm), feeding a few times a week is possible. Otherwise feed more often (5–6 times a week). Do not overfeed: overfeeding is one of the biggest causes of death for dwarf shrimp, and it is worse for sensitive species like this one. Uneaten food decomposes and can cause infections, parasites, and ammonia, nitrite and nitrate spikes. It is better to underfeed than overfeed.

Despite the predatory name, Leopard shrimp are completely harmless and will not bother anything in a community tank. They are social and prefer large groups, which makes their life less stressful. They are very shy, especially in small groups; the bigger the colony, the more confident they are and the more often they come out of hiding.

They are nocturnal: activity peaks at sunset and gradually stops before sunrise. In nature this is associated with avoiding visual predators while feeding.
Because of their transparent body, the female's saddle (on the upper body, behind the head, where eggs are stored before fertilization) is easy to see.

Depending on temperature, Leopard shrimp mature at about 3–3.5 months old. Females molt before mating and release a chemical substance into the water to attract males, which then swim in frenzied circuits seeking her. Mating is very brief, a few seconds.

Some females can carry up to 59 eggs, which they keep for the whole incubation, usually 4 to 6 weeks. There are no larval stages: what emerges from the egg is a tiny copy of the adult.

Balance their feeding with powdered food. Baby shrimp do not move around as much as adults, so they starve if they do not find enough food nearby.
